title: 12 Effects of partially replacing steam-flaked corn with high moisture rolled sorghum on dry matter intake and rumination time of finishing beef steers
content:
Abstract
High moisture sorghum may represent a viable alternative to replace corn grain in the diet of beef and dairy cattle in semiarid regions. Compared to corn, sorghum is a crop that requires less water, providing a low-cost input and water-efficient option for grain in areas with water scarcity. The objective of the study was to evaluate the effects of partially replacing steam-flaked corn (SFC) with high moisture rolled sorghum grain (HMRS) on dry matter (DM) intake (DMI) and daily rumination time (DRT) of finishing cattle. A total of 20 metric tons of high-moisture sorghum grain were harvested in the Texas Panhandle at the physiological maturity stage (hard dough) with 28% humidity. A R990MXPlus Roller Mill Bagger was used to process and bag the grain in a silo bag with 2.7 m of diameter, which was stored for 314 days before the beginning of the experiment. Twelve cannulated Angus-crossbred steers [body weight (BW) = 774 ± 63 kg] were used in a quadruplicated 3 × 3 Latin Square (LS) design to evaluate 3 levels of replacement of SFC with HMRS. Treatments were: control diet (HMRS0): 11% roughage (corn stalks) and 89% concentrate (63.3% SFC, 20% Sweet bran, 0.7% urea, 2% corn oil, and 3% mineral and vitamin premix), replacing 25% of the SFC in 0HMRS diet with HMRS (i.e., 47.48% SFC and 15.83% HMS; HMRS25), and replacing 50% of the SFC in HMRS0 diet (i.e., 31.65% SFC and 31.65% HMS; HMRS50). Each experimental period included 15 days of adaptation and 6 days of sampling. Steers were fed ad libitum once a day and refusals were collected and weighed daily before the morning feeding. Samples of experimental diets and refusals were collected and dried for DM determination and DMI calculation. Rumination time (DRT) was measured using SCRHeatime collars. Data was analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS with treatment as the predictor variable and LS, period (LS), and steer (LS) as random effects. The contrast statement of SAS was used to assess treatment linear and quadratic effects. Treatments did not affect DMI (P = 0.32, linear P = 0.14, quadratic P = 0.85) and DRT (P = 0.39, linear P = 0.57, quadratic P = 0.22). The least square means (LSM) for DMI (± 0.99 kg/day) and DRT (± 37 min/day) for HMRS0, HMRS25 and HMRS50 diets were 15.77, 15.96 and 16.25 kg/d and 383, 400 and 370 minutes/d, respectively. These data suggest that partially replacing SFC with HMRS may not significantly increase DMI or rumination behavior.
